hints: Find the intersection of $y^2 = x - 2$ and $y = 1$ to obtain the lower integration limit $x = 3$.
Set up the volume integral $V = \pi \int_3^5 (y_{\text{curve}}^2 - y_{\text{line}}^2)\,dx$.
walkthrough:
Find the lower limit of integration where the curve $y^2 = x - 2$ meets the line $y = 1$:
$$1^2 = x - 2 \implies x = 3$$

Set up the volume of revolution about the $x$-axis using the difference of squared functions:
$$V = \pi \int_3^5 \left(y_{\text{curve}}^2 - y_{\text{line}}^2\right) dx = \pi \int_3^5 \left[(x - 2) - 1^2\right] dx = \pi \int_3^5 (x - 3)\,dx$$

Integrate and apply the fundamental theorem of calculus:
$$V = \pi \left[\frac{1}{2}x^2 - 3x\right]_3^5$$

Evaluate at limits $x = 5$ and $x = 3$:
$$\text{At } x = 5:\quad \frac{25}{2} - 15 = -\frac{5}{2}$$
$$\text{At } x = 3:\quad \frac{9}{2} - 9 = -\frac{9}{2}$$
$$V = \pi \left[-\frac{5}{2} - \left(-\frac{9}{2}\right)\right] = \pi \left(\frac{4}{2}\right) = 2\pi \approx 6.28$$

ai_rubric.Volume of Revolution: Finds intersection limit $x = 3$ (B1), sets up volume integral $\pi \int_3^5 (x-3)\,dx$ (M1B1), integrates correctly (A1), applies limits (M1), and obtains $2\pi$ (or approx $6.28$) (A1).
